cards.text: This psalm opens with one big word: "Hallelujah!" Then the writer turns and talks to himself: "Praise the LORD, O my soul." Friend, that's a man giving his own soul a pep talk, and I RESPECT it, because I gave myself plenty of those in the back of a junk drawer.

cards.question: Right away, the writer makes a promise about praising the LORD. How long does he say he'll keep it up?

cards.text: Then the psalm slams on the brakes. Praise is on hold for one second, because here comes a warning about who NOT to lean on.

cards.question: The psalm warns: Put not your trust in ___.
In this warning, the psalm calls princes mortal men who cannot save. True or false?

cards.text: And here's what mortal looks like. When a man's spirit departs, he returns to the ground, crown and all.

cards.question: The psalm says that when a prince dies, his plans live on after him. True or false?

cards.text: The five-year plan, the big strategy, the corner office? GONE, that very same day. Then the psalm flips it around: there IS a help worth having.

cards.question: The psalm says blessed is the one whose help comes from whom?

cards.text: The prince goes back to the ground, but the God of Jacob is the One who MADE the ground. The psalm calls Him "the Maker of heaven and earth, the sea, and everything in them."

cards.question: The psalm says the LORD stays faithful only as long as His people stay faithful. True or false?

cards.text: Now the psalm rolls out what this God actually does. Friend, I have never seen a résumé like this, and I've seen an expired coupon brag about itself for YEARS.

cards.question: First on the LORD's list: what does He do for the oppressed?
The list keeps going. The LORD gives food to the ___ and sets the ___ free.

cards.text: The LORD opens the eyes of the blind and lifts those who are weighed down. I spent years under a stack of old takeout menus, so that second one? PERSONAL.

cards.question: In the same verse, the psalm names who the LORD loves. Who is it?

cards.text: The LORD protects foreigners, and He sustains the fatherless and the widow. But not everybody in this psalm gets a helping hand.

cards.question: What does the LORD do to the ways of the wicked?
A prince's plans perish the day he dies. But the psalm ends this way: The LORD reigns ___, your God, O Zion, for all generations.

cards.text: And the psalm signs off right where it started: "Hallelujah!" Same word at the front door and the back door, friend, so praise gets the first word AND the last word.

findings.problem: Papa Dorin says he gave himself plenty of pep talks in the junk drawer. The backstory doesn't say this. It actually says he gave up on himself and didn't talk much, so the line adds something new to his story and goes against it.

rule.text: His own world isn't Bible fact. His backstory, family, bakery and mission are the Dorinverse story in this file. He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them.

findings.problem: The fill in the blank asks the baker to finish the line 'Put not your trust in ___' with princes, prophets or priests. Nothing on the earlier cards lets the baker reason this out. It tests wording they haven't seen.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: Jacob appears here (and in the card 9 answer) without a simple word on who he is.

rule.text: The first time someone shows up, he says simply who they are, like "Cyrus, king of Persia" or "Moses, Israel's leader."

findings.problem: The joke mentions 'an expired coupon' without saying it was in the drawer he shared. Bakers don't know about the coupon, so the callback won't land. Calling the coupon a bragger also stretches what the backstory says about it.

rule.text: Bakers know he spent years in a junk drawer, from onboarding. The drawer's small details, like the batteries, the key or the coupon, only come up when the line says what they are, like "the dead batteries I shared that drawer with."

findings.problem: The wrong word 'servants' can be argued as right. 'Sets the servants free' and 'gives food to the servants' both sound like things the LORD does, so a baker could argue for either one.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: The setup line 'not everybody in this psalm gets a helping hand' rules out the wrong answer 'He makes them prosper' on card 18 before the baker answers.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.
